883.title: Bezalel the craftsman
883.hook: Bezalel is filled with spirit to work in gold, stone and wood (Exodus 31:1–5)
883.howItsDone: Some Jewish and Christian readers point to Bezalel when they speak of craft and art as a gift of the spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was six days: work, then a stop for everyone within the gates. Your line was fairness, written into the week.

The plans are already given: curtains, a chest, a lampstand, a tent of worship, all of it to be made by hand, out in the wilderness. In the book of Exodus, Moses has been shown the design. What they need now is someone who can do the work. A jeweler's eye. A stonemason's straight line. A carpenter's palm that feels what the eye misses. God calls a craftsman by name. Today: Bezalel.
screen: `THE PLANS ARE GIVEN.` → `A TENT TO BE MADE BY HAND.` → `A CRAFTSMAN, CALLED BY NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the call. “See, I have called by name Bezaleel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.” The King James spells it Bezaleel. He's named with his father, his father's father and his tribe. The one who works with his hands is not anonymous labor. He's called by name. Second, the gift. “And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship.” Then the text says what it's for: to work in gold and silver and brass, to cut and set stones, to carve timber. Here the spirit of God doesn't arrive as a vision or a voice. It arrives in the hands. Wisdom, in this chapter, includes knowing how to set a stone straight. Third, the teaching. A few chapters on, the text says he was given it in his heart to teach, he and a partner named Aholiab. The skill isn't a secret to hoard. It's handed on, from one pair of hands to the next. Fourth, the edge from yesterday. Right after Bezalel is named, the same chapter turns back to the sabbath: “Verily my sabbaths ye shall keep.” Some readers, the medieval commentator Rashi among them, take the order as a lesson: even the work of building a holy place stops on the seventh day. So craft, in Exodus, is holy, and it still rests. A careful weld, a well-cut sleeve, a cake with straight layers: a reader of this chapter could call any of them a gift of the spirit.

segments.voice: Rest your hands and feel them, the fingertips, the palms, the small muscles you only notice when they're tired; these hands have made meals, notes, repairs. Bring to mind one small, real thing they could make today, a sandwich made with care, a sewn-on button, a card, and picture the very first motion. If you pray, you can hold that making in your own tradition's words.
Bezalel. The craftsman called by name in Exodus and filled with the spirit of God to work in gold, stone and wood. Today's word.
Your line: craft is holy. And even holy work rests. That's day eight hundred eighty-three.

884.title: Go to the ant
884.hook: go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways (Proverbs 6:6)
884.carry: steady effort, at the right time
884.howItsDone: Some Jewish and Christian teachers use Proverbs 6:6 to teach diligence, sometimes alongside the lazy man of Proverbs 26, and the Qur'an names a surah for the ant.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Bezalel, filled with the spirit to work in gold, stone and wood. Your line was craft is holy.

A line of ants crosses a kitchen counter, each one hauling a crumb bigger than its head. One response is a sponge. The book of Proverbs has another: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.” Not a king, not a sage, not a prophet. The teacher, for once, is tiny, and the student is someone who can't get out of bed. Today: an-Naml.
screen: `A LINE OF ANTS ON THE COUNTER.` → `CONSIDER HER WAYS.` → `A VERY SMALL TEACHER.`

segments.voice: First, meet the sluggard. Proverbs has fun with him. He won't go out, he says, because there's a lion in the street. And then: “As the door turneth upon his hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.” Turning and turning, going nowhere. The laugh is aimed at a habit, not at a person. Second, no boss. The ant, Proverbs says, works “having no guide, overseer, or ruler.” Nobody stands over her with a clipboard. That's the lesson aimed at the sluggard: not more supervision, but his own reason to get up. Third, timing. The ant “provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.” She works while the work can be done, so that later there's enough. Some work can't be crammed into the night before. Fourth, small and wise. Later in Proverbs the ants come back, in a list of creatures “little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise.” They are “a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer.” Wisdom here isn't size or strength. It's steady effort, at the right time, with nobody watching. The ant has a neighbor's echo, too: in the Qur'an, a surah is named for the ant, an-Naml. In it, an ant calls to the others to get out of the way of Solomon's army, and Solomon smiles at her words.

segments.voice: Find something small at work nearby, ants on a path, a bird carrying a twig, rain filling a gutter, the second hand of a clock, or bring one to mind, and watch it without hurrying it: the small motion, repeated, steady, waiting for no one's permission. Let your breath settle to its pace, and let one small piece of your own work come to mind, before the season for it passes. If you pray, you can hold it in your own tradition's words.

Your line: steady effort, at the right time. No overseer needed, and nobody watching. Until tomorrow.

885.title: Eat and enjoy
885.hook: Ecclesiastes: nothing better than to eat and drink and enjoy your labor (Ecclesiastes 2:24)
885.howItsDone: Some Jewish communities read Ecclesiastes aloud during Sukkot, the harvest festival, and Jewish and Christian readers return to its eat-and-drink verses when they speak of enjoying the fruit of work as a gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was an-Naml, the surah named for the ant; Proverbs' ant needs no overseer. Your line was steady effort, at the right time.

“Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.” That's the Preacher's opening cry in Ecclesiastes. Then he keeps going: the sun rises and sets, the rivers run into the sea and the sea is never full, one generation goes and another comes. A reader could expect the book to end with, so why bother. Instead, right in the middle of all that weariness, it keeps saying something surprising. Eat. Drink. Enjoy your work. Today: Sukkot.
screen: `VANITY OF VANITIES.` → `THE SEA IS NEVER FULL.` → `AND YET: EAT, DRINK, ENJOY.`

segments.voice: First, the gloom is honest. The Preacher has tried everything: building houses, planting vineyards, gathering silver and gold. Looking back on it all, he says: “all was vanity and vexation of spirit.” He doesn't pretend work saves anyone from death, and that honesty is why what comes next carries weight. Second, the turn, in the same chapter: “There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour.” Notice where the good is found. Not after the work, in some distant retirement. In the labor itself. Third, the source. The verse continues: “This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God.” In the next chapter he says it again: to eat and drink and enjoy the good of all your labor “is the gift of God.” Enjoyment, in this book, isn't a wage you earn by working hard enough. It's a gift you're allowed to take. Fourth, how. Later the Preacher puts it almost as an instruction: “Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart.” Bread, wine, a table: the ordinary fruit of ordinary work. Some Jewish communities read Ecclesiastes aloud during Sukkot, the harvest festival of booths. A book that knows everything passes, read at a harvest feast, saying: enjoy the harvest while it's here.
screen: `ALL IS VANITY.` · `NOTHING BETTER THAN THIS.` · `A GIFT, NOT A WAGE.` · `EAT THY BREAD WITH JOY.` · then, large: `ENJOY THE LABOR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one fruit of your own work, a meal, a clean room, a rent payment that went through, a child's packed lunch, and notice what's good about it without reaching for the list of what's still undone. If a cup or a piece of fruit is within reach, you can taste it now, slowly. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words.
Sukkot. The Jewish harvest festival of booths, when some communities read Ecclesiastes aloud, praising the good found in labor. Today's word.
Your line: enjoy the labor. A gift, not a wage. Day eight hundred eighty-five counts.

886.title: Not yours to finish
886.hook: Rabbi Tarfon: it is not yours to finish the work, nor are you free to stop (Pirkei Avot 2:16)
886.howItsDone: Pirkei Avot is studied in Jewish communities as a book of ethics, and Rabbi Tarfon's saying is one people turn to when a task feels too large to finish.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Sukkot, when some communities read the Preacher's surprise: find good in your labor. Your line was enjoy the labor.

Some work is too big for one life. A cathedral raised stone by stone. A row of oaks planted for shade the planter won't sit in. A cure. A fair city. A child raised into a future the parent won't see the end of. Work that size offers two easy answers: try to do it all yourself, or decide it's hopeless and do nothing. A rabbi in the Mishnah turns down both, in a single sentence. Today: Pirkei Avot.
screen: `A CATHEDRAL. A ROW OF OAKS.` → `TOO BIG FOR ONE LIFE.` → `TWO EASY ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, is a part of the Mishnah gathered from short sayings of the early rabbis. Two of Rabbi Tarfon's sayings sit side by side. The first is a quick, urgent picture: the day is short, the work is great, the workers are sluggish, the reward is much, and the master of the house is pressing. It sounds like a busy workshop at closing time. It's also a picture of a life. Second, the release. Then Tarfon says: it is not upon you to finish the work. That's a mercy. No single person has to repair the whole world, end every injustice, or get every child grown and safe. Third, the catch. In the same breath he adds: but neither are you free to walk away from it. The release isn't permission to quit. You can't finish, and you can't stop. Both halves, held together, the way a sabbath held work and rest together a few days ago. Fourth, what that leaves: your part, a shift in a long relay. This week's voices have been circling it: a garden tended before you came and after you go, a craftsman who teaches what he knows, an ant gathering for a season it may not see. Tarfon names the shape. The whole isn't yours. The piece in front of you is.
screen: `THE DAY IS SHORT, THE WORK IS GREAT.` · `NOT YOURS TO FINISH.` · `NOR FREE TO STOP.` · `YOUR PART OF THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `NOT MINE TO FINISH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something huge you care about that you'll never finish alone, a family's healing, a neighborhood, the health of the earth, and let it be as big as it is. Then, inside that bigness, find one small part that's yours this week, a call, an hour, a page, and hold it in mind until it's concrete. If you pray, you can hold it in your own tradition's words.

887.title: The carpenter
887.hook: Jesus is called a carpenter by his neighbors (Mark 6:3)
887.howItsDone: Christians read Mark 6 as part of the Gospel, and some churches hold prayers or blessings for workers; Catholics keep a feast of St Joseph the Worker.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Pirkei Avot, where Rabbi Tarfon says the work isn't yours to finish, and you aren't free to stop. Your line was not mine to finish.

His own country, Mark calls it. On the sabbath day a local man stands up in the synagogue to teach, and Mark's Gospel says the hearers were astonished. Where did he get all this? Then the question comes out loud, and the King James Bible keeps it word for word: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary." They know him. They name his mother, his brothers, his sisters. And because they know him, they can't hear him. Today's word is the job his neighbors gave him.
screen: `A SABBATH IN HIS HOMETOWN.` → `WHERE DID HE GET THIS?` → `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?`

segments.voice: Start with the word itself. Mark doesn't introduce Jesus as a carpenter. His neighbors do, almost as a put-down. In Mark the line is "Is not this the carpenter." In Matthew's telling of the same scene it becomes "Is not this the carpenter's son?" So one Gospel gives the trade to Jesus, and another gives it to Joseph. Readers have noticed the difference, and some simply hear both: a family trade, passed from father to son. Second, the silence. The Gospels never tell us what he built. No tables, no doorframes, no workshop scenes. The text gives one word and stops. Third, what the neighbors do with it. Mark says, "they were offended at him." Familiar hands, an ordinary trade, and so the wisdom can't be real. Jesus answers: "A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country." Fourth, why the word lingers. Christians say Jesus is God made flesh, and some find meaning in the fact that, before any teaching, he had a trade, and he worked with his hands. Catholics honor Joseph with a feast of St Joseph the Worker. Whatever a listener believes about Jesus, the word sits there as a quiet challenge: the people who build and fix and carry are easy to look past, the way his neighbors looked past the wisdom to the trade.
screen: `HIS NEIGHBORS NAME THE TRADE.` · `THE GOSPELS NEVER SAY WHAT HE BUILT.` · `THEY WERE OFFENDED AT HIM.` · `HANDS THAT WORKED.` · then, large: `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?`

segments.voice: Look around, or picture the room: someone built the chair under you, laid the floor, ran the wires, stitched the clothes you're wearing. Pick one of them, a person whose name you'll never know, and picture their hands at work, the dust, the ache at the end of the day; breathe in what they made possible for you, and breathe out thanks. If you pray, you can hold that worker in your own tradition's words.
The carpenter. What his hometown called Jesus when it couldn't believe the wisdom coming from a man who worked with his hands. Today's word.
Your line: easy to look past. Someone's hands built the room you're in. That's day eight hundred eighty-seven.

888.title: Martha and Mary
888.hook: Martha is busy serving; Mary sits and listens, and Jesus says she chose the good part (Luke 10:38–42)
888.howItsDone: Christians read Luke 10:38–42 as a call to make time to listen to God, and some retreat houses and prayer groups use Mary's sitting at Jesus' feet as a picture of quiet prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the carpenter: his neighbors named his trade and couldn't hear his wisdom. Your line was easy to look past.

"Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone?" That's Martha, in Luke's Gospel, and she has a point. Jesus has come to her village and she has opened her home. There's a guest to feed, and a house to run. And her sister Mary is sitting on the floor at Jesus' feet, listening, not lifting a finger. She goes straight to the guest and asks him to send her sister in to help. His answer is not the one she wants.
screen: `A FULL KITCHEN.` → `A SISTER ON THE FLOOR.` → `TELL HER TO HELP ME.`

segments.voice: Luke says Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word," while "Martha was cumbered about much serving." Cumbered: weighed down, pulled in every direction. Then the answer, gentle, her name said twice: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her." First, notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't tell Martha that cooking is wrong, or that she should stop serving guests. He names the worry. Second, the one thing. Luke doesn't spell it out. What the text shows is Mary sitting and hearing his word, and Christians usually read the one thing as that listening. The King James says that good part; other English Bibles say the better part, which is where today's line comes from. Third, Martha is not the villain. In John's Gospel, when her brother Lazarus has died, it's Martha who goes out to meet Jesus on the road and says, "I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God." Some Christian writers have read the two sisters as two ways of life, active service and quiet prayer, and have argued about which matters more. Others say a life needs both, and that even Martha's kitchen can be holy. Fourth, the modern house. Busy work fills every gap: the dishes, the inbox, the small urgent tasks that feel like duty. The story asks a quiet question: is there a better part you're too busy to sit down for?
screen: `MARTHA, MARTHA.` · `ONE THING IS NEEDFUL.` · `MARTHA IS NOT THE VILLAIN.` · `TOO BUSY TO SIT DOWN.` · then, large: `MARY HATH CHOSEN THAT GOOD PART.`

segments.voice: For the next two minutes, be Mary: put down whatever you were about to do, and simply listen, to the sounds in the room, the sounds outside it, your own breath going in and out. When you drift back into the kitchen, planning, tidying, answering, smile at Martha and come back to the floor. If you pray, this can be a time of listening in your own tradition's way.
Martha. The sister in Luke's Gospel busy serving in her kitchen, while Mary sat at Jesus' feet and heard his word. Today's word.
Your line: the better part. One thing is needful, and Mary chose it. Day eight hundred eighty-eight, done.

889.title: The tentmaker
889.hook: Paul supports himself making tents while he travels (Acts 18:3)
889.howItsDone: Some Christians call working an ordinary job while sharing their faith 'tentmaking', after Paul in Acts 18.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Martha, busy serving while her sister Mary sat to listen. Your line was the better part.

The book of Acts is full of riots, shipwrecks and prison doors. Then, in Corinth, it slows down long enough to mention a job. A traveling teacher arrives in the city and finds a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla, lately come from Italy. They share a trade. So he moves in with them and goes to work: a bench, his hands, the day's labor. Then, every sabbath, he goes to the synagogue to reason with whoever will listen. The man is Paul, and the book that tells his travels pauses to name his day job.
screen: `A JOB IN CORINTH.` → `A COUPLE WITH THE SAME TRADE.` → `A BENCH, THEN THE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: First, the verse itself, in the King James Bible: "And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers." Wrought is the old word for worked. Paul isn't visiting a workshop. He's in it. Second, why he did it. Later in Acts, saying goodbye to friends from Ephesus, Paul holds up his hands: "Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me." In his own letters he says he had a right to be supported by the people he taught, and chose not to use it, so that nothing would hinder the gospel and he could offer it without charge. Third, what the text leaves out. Acts doesn't describe the work at all: no tools, no customers, no hours. It names the trade and moves on. What it makes plain is that the teacher worked, and wasn't ashamed to say so. Fourth, the people beside him. Aquila and Priscilla aren't just landlords. In Acts and in Paul's letters they appear again as teachers and friends, partners in the work as much as in the trade. Some Christians today borrow the word itself. They call someone a tentmaker when they carry their faith into an ordinary job and pay their own way, rather than being paid to preach. Paul's letters also thank the church at Philippi for gifts sent to him, so he did sometimes accept help. But in Corinth, Acts shows him at the bench, working with his hands.
screen: `OF THE SAME CRAFT, HE WROUGHT.` · `THESE HANDS HAVE MINISTERED.` · `THE MESSAGE FREE, HIS OWN WAY PAID.` · `PARTNERS AT THE BENCH.` · then, large: `BY THEIR OCCUPATION THEY WERE TENTMAKERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that someone else quietly pays for or does for you, a ride, a bill, a meal, a chore that's drifted onto someone else's plate, and just notice it, with no guilt. Then ask what one piece of it you could take back this week, and breathe with that. If you pray, you can offer your hands and their work in your own tradition's words.
The tentmaker. Paul's trade, according to Acts: working with Aquila and Priscilla, paying his own way while he taught. Today's word.
Your line: work with my hands. The message free, his own way paid. Until tomorrow.
